_meta.title: Διάδοχοι — the heads of Plato's school, 387 BCE – 529 CE
_meta.note: Succession order, headship dates, and birthplaces after the project infographic. 'heads' are scholarchs of the Academy (nos. 1–15) and of the Neoplatonist school that revived it in Athens (nos. 16–21, with Hegias uncertain). 'platonists' are notable Platonists who taught at Athens during the ~490-year gap but were not heads.
_meta.unplotted: Carneades the Younger (no. 12), Ammonius (Attica or Egypt), and Atticus (origin unknown) have no securely recorded birthplace and are not mapped.
_meta.sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives, Book 4; Philodemus, Index Academicorum; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Smith, Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography.

heads.name: Plato
heads.bio: Founded the Academy around 387 BCE in a grove sacred to the hero Academus. His dialogues and the theory of Forms set the agenda for the school and for much of later philosophy.
heads.note: Some ancient sources give his birthplace as Aegina rather than Athens.

heads.name: Speusippus
heads.bio: Plato's nephew, who succeeded him as head. He revised the theory of Forms toward mathematical principles and is said to have resigned through ill health.

heads.name: Xenocrates
heads.bio: A systematizer who divided philosophy into physics, ethics, and logic and defended a metaphysics of Forms-as-numbers. He led the school for twenty-five years.

heads.name: Polemo
heads.bio: Converted from a dissolute youth to philosophy on hearing Xenocrates, and as head insisted that philosophy be lived, not merely argued. Zeno of Citium, founder of Stoicism, studied under him.

heads.name: Crates of Athens
heads.bio: Pupil and close companion of Polemo, whom he briefly succeeded. Little of his own teaching survives.

heads.name: Arcesilaus
heads.bio: Turned the Academy toward skepticism, reviving Socratic questioning and arguing that one should suspend judgment, since nothing can be known with certainty. Founder of what later writers called the Middle Academy.

heads.name: Lacydes
heads.bio: Led the school in the period later called the New Academy and reputedly taught in a garden given by king Attalus. He continued the skeptical line.

heads.name: Telecles
heads.bio: A head of the skeptical Academy in the early 2nd century BCE, known chiefly from the succession lists.
heads.note: Modern editors of Diogenes Laertius read Phocaea; older texts read Phocis, in Greece.

heads.name: Evander
heads.bio: A head of the Academy around the same time as Telecles; little beyond his place in the succession is recorded.
heads.note: Phocaea/Phocis is disputed in the sources, as with Telecles.

heads.name: Hegesinus
heads.bio: Head of the Academy shortly before Carneades, known only by name from the succession lists.

heads.name: Carneades
heads.bio: The most formidable skeptic to lead the Academy. On a famous embassy to Rome in 155 BCE he argued brilliantly for justice one day and against it the next, and he refined skepticism into a theory of the 'probable' as a guide to life.

heads.name: Carneades the Younger
heads.bio: A short-serving head between the elder Carneades and Crates of Tarsus. His birthplace is not recorded.

heads.name: Crates of Tarsus
heads.bio: Led the Academy briefly in the 120s BCE; little is known beyond his place in the succession.

heads.name: Clitomachus
heads.bio: Born at Carthage and originally named Hasdrubal, he came to Athens and became Carneades' devoted recorder, writing some four hundred books that preserved his teacher's arguments.

heads.name: Philo of Larissa
heads.bio: The last undisputed head of the Academy. When the Mithridatic war threatened Athens he moved to Rome in 88 BCE, where Cicero heard him; he softened Academic skepticism toward a mitigated fallibilism.

heads.name: Plutarch of Athens
heads.bio: Revived Platonic teaching at Athens around 400 CE as the first head of the Neoplatonist school, and taught Syrianus and the young Proclus.
heads.note: Of an Athenian family; his exact birthplace is not recorded.

heads.name: Syrianus
heads.bio: Head after Plutarch and teacher of Proclus. His commentaries read Aristotle's Metaphysics through a Platonic lens.

heads.name: Proclus
heads.bio: The great systematizer of late Neoplatonism, whose Elements of Theology sets out the whole emanationist cosmos in geometric propositions. He led the school for nearly fifty years.
heads.note: Born at Constantinople and raised in Lycian Xanthus.

heads.name: Marinus
heads.bio: Succeeded Proclus and wrote the Life of Proclus that is our main source for the school. A Samaritan from Neapolis who turned to Hellenism.

heads.name: Isidore
heads.bio: A Neoplatonist head whose life Damascius later recorded; he favored intuitive piety over elaborate system-building.

heads.name: Hegias
heads.bio: May have led the school around 500 CE; the sources are uncertain, and under him the school's fortunes are said to have declined.
heads.note: Whether and exactly when Hegias was head is uncertain.

heads.name: Damascius
heads.bio: The last head of the Athenian school. When Justinian barred pagans from teaching in 529 CE the Academy closed, and Damascius and his circle briefly sought refuge at the Persian court.

platonists.name: Antiochus of Ascalon
platonists.headship: taught at Athens · not a head
platonists.bio: Broke with Academic skepticism around 90 BCE and taught a dogmatic 'Old Academy' blending Plato, Aristotle, and the Stoa. Cicero attended his lectures.

platonists.name: Aristus of Ascalon
platonists.headship: taught at Athens · not a head
platonists.bio: Brother and successor of Antiochus as a teacher at Athens, though not head of an institutional Academy.

platonists.name: Calvenus Taurus
platonists.headship: taught at Athens · not a head
platonists.bio: A leading Platonist teacher at Athens in the 2nd century CE, known for commentaries and for the philosophical dinners described by Aulus Gellius.

platonists.name: Longinus
platonists.headship: taught at Athens · not a head
platonists.bio: A 3rd-century CE critic and Platonist teacher, later minister to queen Zenobia of Palmyra; Plotinus called him 'a scholar, but no philosopher.'
